quote: 20.1 Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer, its Affiliates, and their directors, officers, employees, and agents from each third-party claim and resulting damages, settlements, judgments, penalties, costs, and reasonable attorneys' fees arising from an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate an intellectual property right.
rationale:
Section 20 meets and in places exceeds our preferred position, so no redline is warranted.

(1) Vendor IP indemnity (20.1): Vendor defends and indemnifies Customer, its Affiliates and their directors, officers, employees and agents against third-party claims that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate IP. It runs to affiliates as required, and notably carries none of the usual customer-modification/combination/specification exclusions — better than even the fallback.

(2) Misconduct limbs (20.2): Vendor also indemnifies for its breach of Applicable Law, bodily injury/death/tangible property damage, unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor, and Vendor's gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud. This captures every limb of the preferred position (b)–(d) plus a bodily-injury limb in our favour.

(3) Customer's indemnity is appropriately narrow (20.3): confined to unmodified Customer-supplied material used strictly as authorized, and Customer's violation of Applicable Law in its authorized use — with express carve-outs where the claim arises from Vendor Technology, modification, combination or instructions. That matches the "Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law" ceiling.

(4) Standard procedure (20.4): prompt notice, cooperation at the indemnifying Party's expense, and control of defence, with delay excusing obligations only to the extent of material prejudice, and a settlement-consent protection barring admissions of fault, non-monetary obligations, or failure to fully release us.

(5) Infringement remedies (20.5): procure, modify/replace without materially reducing functionality, or terminate and refund — expressly "in addition to its defence obligations," and Vendor may not terminate unaffected Services.

Cross-check on interactions: the fallback's 3× super-cap is unnecessary because Section 21.3 makes "its indemnification obligations" an Excluded Claim, so Vendor's indemnity sits outside both the 21.1 monetary cap and the 21.2 consequential-damages waiver — i.e., uncapped, which is stronger than the fallback. Sections 19.4 and 19.5 confirm the warranty remedy "is not exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security, or indemnified claims" and that no disclaimer limits an indemnity, so nothing converts 20.5 into a sole-remedy limitation. I searched for "sole and exclusive remedy" and found no such language, and Section 1 contains no competing definition that narrows these terms.

Separately noted for other rules, not this one: the definition of "Fees" (1.7/1.8) is limited to the USD 12,000 Implementation Fee and the 21.1 cap base references only the first Order Form. Those are cap-base concerns under the limitation-of-liability rule and do not affect the indemnity, which is uncapped as an Excluded Claim.

quote: 14.2 Upon creation and subject to payment of the applicable Fees, Customer owns each Deliverable created specifically for Customer. Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all worldwide right, title, and interest in those Deliverables and shall obtain equivalent assignments from its personnel.
rationale: The IP allocation matches our preferred position. Section 14.2 vests each Deliverable in Customer with an express present assignment from Vendor plus personnel assignments and further-assurance support. Section 14.1 confirms Customer owns all Customer Data, Customer Confidential Information and independently developed IP, with no transfer to Vendor beyond a limited processing right; the Customer Data definition (1.3) is broad and includes derived output, excluding only anonymized telemetry. Vendor retains only Vendor Technology (14.3), and any Vendor Technology embedded in a Deliverable is covered by the perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence in Section 13.2 (including modification and derivative works, transferable under 13.3). Section 14.2/14.4 create no joint ownership absent a separate signed instrument, and feedback use is limited with Customer retaining unrestricted rights in its own feedback. No assignment of Customer IP or data to Vendor appears anywhere in the document.
ruleTitle: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The cap is currently measured by "Fees", which is defined as the one-time USD 12,000 Implementation Fee under the first Order Form, so the mutual cap is illusory. We have changed the basis to all amounts paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim, with a USD 1,000,000 floor, per our standard position; Excluded Claims (indemnities, confidentiality, data protection and security, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement) remain outside the cap. If the USD 1,000,000 floor is an issue, we can accept a straight 12 months' amounts cap.

ops.newText: shall not exceed the greater of (a) all amounts paid or payable by Customer under this Agreement and all Order Forms during the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim and (b) USD 1,000,000.
ops.oldText: shall not exceed the Fees paid or payable by Customer under the first Order Form during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim.

proposal.summary: Replace the illusory "Fees"/first Order Form cap basis with the greater of 12 months' amounts paid or payable and USD 1,000,000.

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the Fees paid or payable by Customer under the first Order Form during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: The cap is mutual and the carve-outs (Excluded Claims in 21.3: confidentiality, data protection/security, indemnities, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud, IP infringement) and the mutual consequential-damages exclusion in 21.2 match our preferred position, and Customer's payment obligation is expressly excluded from the cap. The defect is the cap basis: "Fees" is defined (1.5/1.6) as the one-time USD 12,000 Implementation Fee stated in the first Order Form, so the aggregate cap is effectively USD 12,000 — far below 6 months' actual spend and an illusory cap in Vendor's favour. Redline changes the basis to all amounts paid or payable under the Agreement and all Order Forms in the 12 months preceding the claim, with a USD 1,000,000 floor; fallback is a straight 12 months' amounts cap.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

quote: 24.1 Customer may assign this Agreement or an Order Form without Vendor's consent to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.
rationale: Section 24 meets the preferred position in full: 24.1 gives Customer an unqualified right to assign to an Affiliate or M&A successor without Vendor consent (notice only); 24.2 bars Vendor assignment, delegation of material performance, or transfer by change of control without Customer's consent (reasonableness standard running in our favour) and bars assignment to a direct Customer competitor; 24.3 applies a mutual not-unreasonably-withheld standard to other assignments; and 24.4 expressly denies Vendor any right to terminate, suspend, reprice, accelerate Fees, or reduce service on Customer's change of control, with a cooperation obligation for successor administrative changes. Searches for "assign" and "change of control" across the document found no competing trigger — Section 9 termination contains only a standard mutual insolvency/general-assignment-for-creditors right, and Section 13.x confirms Customer may transfer licence rights to an Affiliate or successor under a Section 24 permitted assignment. "Affiliate" (1.1) uses a conventional >50% control test, so the carve-out is not artificially narrow. No redline needed.

quote: 12.3 Nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service, engaging any supplier, hiring any person who responds to general recruitment, or conducting business in any field or territory. Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: The agreement imposes no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation on Customer. Section 12.3 expressly confirms Customer may engage any supplier and has made no exclusivity, non-compete, or minimum-volume commitment, and Section 2.1 states there is no minimum quantity or purchase commitment and that declining further Order Forms is not a breach. The only exclusivity-type restraint (12.4, barring Vendor from marketing a directly competing analytics service) runs against Vendor and benefits Customer, which the rule treats as acceptable. Other "exclusive" hits are unrelated (non-exclusive licence in 13, exclusive remedy/jurisdiction language). Preferred position met; no redline needed.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have removed the liquidated damages payable by us on late payment (15% of annual Fees per week) and replaced it with simple late-payment interest, since our playbook does not accept liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer and this charge could quickly exceed the remaining contract value. We are happy to discuss the interest rate or a modest fixed late fee if that helps.

ops.newText: 7.7 If a proper, undisputed invoice is not paid within thirty days after its due date, Vendor's sole remedy is simple interest on the overdue amount at the lesser of one percent per month or the maximum rate permitted by Applicable Law, accruing from the due date until paid. Customer owes no liquidated damages, penalty, or other similar amount under this Agreement.
ops.oldText: 7.7 If any invoice is not paid within ten days of its due date, Customer shall pay Vendor, as liquidated damages and not as a penalty, an amount equal to fifteen percent of the annual Fees for each week the invoice remains unpaid.

proposal.summary: Delete Customer-payable liquidated damages in 7.7 and substitute ordinary late-payment interest.

quote: 7.7 If any invoice is not paid within ten days of its due date, Customer shall pay Vendor, as liquidated damages and not as a penalty, an amount equal to fifteen percent of the annual Fees for each week the invoice remains unpaid.
rationale: Section 7.7 imposes liquidated damages payable by Customer to Vendor for late payment, which the playbook prohibits. The amount (15% of annual Fees per week of delay) is punitive and would rapidly exceed the remaining contract value, putting it in walk-away territory; it also sits uneasily with the dispute-withholding right in 7.3 and the mutual liability cap in 21.1 (which expressly does not limit Fee obligations). No Customer-payable early-termination or minimum fee appears elsewhere (Sections 9 and 21 are clean), so the single fix is to strike the LD and substitute ordinary late-payment interest as Vendor's sole remedy.
ruleTitle: Liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer

quote: 13.3 Customer may transfer its licence rights to an Affiliate or successor in connection with an assignment permitted by Section 24. Vendor shall not revoke or suspend a licence except during a material uncured payment or use breach affecting the licensed item, after notice and a reasonable opportunity to cure.
rationale: Section 13 satisfies every element of the preferred position. Clause 13.1 grants the subscription access right to "Customer, its Affiliates, and contractors acting on their behalf" on a worldwide, non-exclusive basis for internal business purposes, and extends to Authorized Users — so affiliates and contractors are expressly in scope with no need for the fallback notice mechanic. Clause 13.2 makes paid-up and Deliverable-embedded software a "perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence" to Customer and its Affiliates, including modification and derivative-work rights and contractor support. Clause 13.3 confirms transferability to an Affiliate or successor via Section 24, and limits revocation or suspension to a material uncured payment or use breach after notice and a reasonable cure opportunity — i.e., no revocation at Vendor's discretion. Section 24.1 backs this up by allowing Customer to assign to an Affiliate or M&A successor without Vendor's consent, and 24.4 bars Vendor from terminating, repricing, or reducing service on a Customer change of control. The "Affiliate" definition (1.1) is a standard majority-control test that does not narrow the grant. The restrictions in 13.4 are ordinary anti-misuse covenants and are expressly carved back for authorized security testing and Customer Data and output, so they do not undercut the grant. No deviation from the licence-scope rule.

quote: 12.3 Nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service, engaging any supplier, hiring any person who responds to general recruitment, or conducting business in any field or territory. Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: The Agreement contains no non-compete or field-of-use restriction binding us. Section 12.3 affirmatively confirms that nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling or using any product or service, engaging any supplier, or conducting business in any field or territory, and that no exclusivity, non-compete, MFC, minimum-volume or no-hire commitment has been made. The only competition restraint (§ 12.4) binds Vendor, not Customer, and therefore benefits us. Licence restrictions in § 13.4 are ordinary use/anti-abuse limits (reverse engineering, interference, unlawful use) with statutory and security-testing carve-outs, not competitive or field-of-use restraints. No redline needed; this meets the preferred position.

quote: 9.4 Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form without cause by delivering the written notice specified in Section 29.4. Customer owes only accrued Fees, and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees for the period after termination.
rationale: Meets the preferred position in full. Section 9.4 gives Customer a without-cause termination right over the Agreement and any Order Form, with the notice period resolving via Section 29.4 to thirty days before the effective termination date. Customer owes only accrued Fees and Vendor must refund prepaid Fees for the post-termination period, so there is a pro-rata refund and no early-termination fee or penalty. Vendor has no reciprocal convenience right: its only termination rights are mutual for-cause rights for material breach (9.1) and insolvency (9.2), and no Vendor convenience right exists during the three-year term under Section 8.1 (confirmed by a full-document sweep for termination rights; Sections 20.5 and 24.4 further bar Vendor from terminating unaffected Services or terminating on Customer change of control). Section 10 imposes refund duties on Vendor rather than exit charges on Customer. No redline required.

quote: 22.1 Vendor may audit Customer's compliance with licence quantities no more than once in any twelve-month period, on at least thirty days' prior written notice, during normal business hours, and in a manner that does not unreasonably disrupt Customer. An audit will be conducted off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality.
rationale: Section 22 meets every element of the preferred position: frequency capped at once in any twelve-month period (22.1), thirty days' prior written notice (22.1), normal business hours and non-disruption (22.1), off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality (22.1), Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds five percent (22.2), and an express prohibition on direct access to Customer systems, unrelated Customer Data, privileged material and third-party confidential information (22.2). Section 22.3 adds customer-favourable protections (findings are our Confidential Information, use limited to enforcement, copy of the report, and finality on payment of the shortfall). Section 23 (Records and Customer Assurance) contains no operative text, and a document-wide search for audit/inspection/verification/records language found no other audit right binding us. No redline required.

quote: 28.1 This Agreement and each dispute arising from it are governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict-of-law principles.
rationale: Section 28 selects New York law and grants exclusive jurisdiction to the state and federal courts in New York County, matching the preferred position exactly. There is no arbitration provision anywhere in the agreement (no hits for "arbitration") and no competing forum or governing-law language elsewhere, so no offshore seat or foreign venue risk arises despite the Vendor being a UK entity. The carve-out permitting temporary injunctive relief in another court is mutual and customary, and the pre-filing executive escalation in 28.2/28.3 does not delay urgent relief or limitations filings. No redline needed.

quote: 7.6 Vendor warrants that Fees charged to Customer will be no less favourable than fees offered to any similarly situated customer for comparable volumes and terms.
rationale: The only MFN-type provision runs in our favour: clause 7.6 obliges Vendor to charge Customer fees no less favourable than those offered to similarly situated customers. There is no obligation on Customer to extend Vendor best terms, match third-party offers, or disclose competitor pricing; clause 12.3 reinforces this by confirming Vendor acknowledges Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment. Searches for MFN, "favourable/favorable", benchmarking and exclusivity language across Sections 7, 12 and 30 found no customer-side MFN. Per the rule's detection guidance, a Vendor-granted MFN is compliant and no redline is proposed.

quote: No minimum quantity or purchase commitment applies. Customer pays only for Services ordered in a mutually executed Order Form, and its decision not to enter another Order Form is not a breach or shortfall.
rationale: Clause 2.1 expressly disclaims any minimum quantity or purchase commitment and confirms Customer pays only for Services actually ordered, with no breach or shortfall for declining further Order Forms — our preferred position. Clause 12.3 reinforces that Customer has given no exclusivity or minimum-volume commitment, and clause 7.1 bars Vendor from imposing minimum-use or similar charges not stated in an Order Form. Sections 4, 7 and 8 contain no committed spend, take-or-pay, shortfall true-up or volume cap on Customer usage; Order Forms renew only in twelve-month increments with a thirty-day non-renewal right (8.2). No redline needed for this rule. (Separately, the liquidated-damages construct in 7.7 is a late-payment penalty issue outside this rule's scope.)
ruleTitle: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer

quote: 12.3 Nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service, engaging any supplier, hiring any person who responds to general recruitment, or conducting business in any field or territory. Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: Searches for "solicit", "induce", "recruit", "hire", "employ" and a review of the likely locations (§ 30 General, § 12 Customer Responsibilities, § 16 Confidentiality) show no non-solicitation, no-hire or anti-poaching covenant binding Northwind. § 12.3 goes further and expressly preserves our freedom to hire any person responding to general recruitment and records that we have made no no-hire commitment. The only forward-looking restriction in § 12 (12.4, non-compete on competing analytics services) binds Vendor and benefits us, so it is not flagged. This matches the preferred position of no non-solicit on Customer; no redline is required.

quote: 8.2 Each Order Form has the initial term stated in it and thereafter renews for successive twelve-month periods unless Customer gives Vendor at least thirty days' written notice of non-renewal. Vendor shall remind Customer of an upcoming renewal at least sixty days beforehand. Failure to send the reminder extends Customer's opt-out deadline until thirty days after the reminder is received.
rationale: Renewals meet the preferred position in full: renewal terms are 12 months (not multi-year), Customer may opt out on only 30 days' written notice, Vendor must send a renewal reminder 60 days beforehand (with the opt-out deadline extended if it fails to do so), and § 8.3 caps renewal uplift at the lesser of CPI and 3% with 90 days' notice and no increase on prepaid periods. The three-year duration in § 8.1 is the initial term of the master agreement, not an automatic multi-year renewal, so the walk-away trigger is not engaged. No conflicting escalation language appears in § 7. No redline needed.

quote: 11.1 Upon expiry or termination for any reason, Vendor shall, at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at the rates in the expiring Order Form. Assistance includes knowledge transfer, export support, cooperation with a replacement supplier, orderly migration, and continued service at the then-current scope and service levels.
rationale: Section 11 meets or exceeds the preferred position on all three elements. (a) Transition assistance: 11.1 gives Customer up to six months of assistance on request, priced at the rates in the expiring Order Form — more favourable to us than the playbook's "then-current rates" — and expressly includes knowledge transfer, export support, cooperation with a replacement supplier, migration, and continued service at existing scope and service levels. (b) Data return: 11.2 requires return of all Customer Data within thirty days in a complete, commonly used, documented, machine-readable format with relationships and metadata, and bars Vendor from holding data hostage over a fee dispute. (c) Deletion and certification: 11.3 sequences deletion only after Customer confirms successful return, limits any retained copy to what Applicable Law requires (protected and use-restricted), and requires written certification by an authorized officer. Cross-checks show no conflict: Section 10.1 preserves Customer Data rights and ends access only after any agreed transition period; Section 15 restricts Vendor's processing; the definition of Customer Data (1.3) is broad; and no suspension, termination (Section 9), or other clause permits immediate deletion or withholding. No redline needed.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return

quote: 19.2 For ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later, each Deliverable will materially conform to its documentation and acceptance criteria. Hosted Services will conform throughout the subscription term. Vendor warrants it has authority to enter the Agreement and grant the rights stated here.
rationale: Section 19 meets or exceeds our preferred position: Vendor warrants professional and workmanlike performance to industry standards (19.1), material conformity of Deliverables for ninety days running from the later of delivery or acceptance and of Hosted Services throughout the subscription term (19.2, i.e. full-term coverage for the software element), plus no-malicious-code and compliance-with-law warranties (19.3). The remedy in 19.4 is repair/replace/re-performance with a termination and refund backstop, and is expressly non-exclusive for fraud, IP, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims — better than the model language, which leaves the remedy at Vendor's option. The only disclaimer (19.5) is mutual, limited to implied warranties, and expressly carves out express warranties, service levels, indemnities and other remedies, so it does not swallow the express warranty. Acceptance (6.1–6.2) and performance (3.1) do not shorten or condition the warranty; acceptance gives an additional correction-and-refund right and the warranty period runs from the later of delivery or acceptance. No redline needed.

quote: 18.1 Vendor shall maintain, at its own expense throughout the term and for one year afterward, commercial general liability insurance of at least USD 1,000,000 per occurrence and USD 2,000,000 aggregate, workers' compensation as required by law, employer's liability of USD 1,000,000, professional errors and omissions insurance of USD 2,000,000, and cyber and privacy liability insurance of USD 5,000,000.
rationale: Section 18 imposes the insurance program on Vendor (Brightline) for our benefit and matches or exceeds our preferred position at every point: CGL of USD 1,000,000 per occurrence / USD 2,000,000 aggregate; professional errors and omissions of USD 2,000,000; cyber and privacy liability of USD 5,000,000 (appropriate given Vendor hosts and processes Customer Data under Sections 15 and 17); and workers' compensation as required by law, plus employer's liability of USD 1,000,000 as an extra. The duration (term plus one year) tracks our model language. Section 18.2 adds the certificate-on-request obligation we require and goes further with reputable-insurer and primary-coverage requirements, advance notice of cancellation or material reduction, and confirmation that insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities (preserving our recovery under Sections 20 and 21). No customer-side burden or coverage gap is present, so no redline is warranted.
